book: 203 - Watchmen and Philosophy - A Rorschach Test

chapters.file: ch03 - A R O R S C H A C H.md
ch04 - C O N T E N T S.md
ch05 - P A R T O N E.md
chapters.relation: Christopher Robichaud's essay asks what morality can demand of Dr. Manhattan after the accident strips him of the moral emotions (in Jesse Prinz's Humean vein) needed to value persons, which is why he can tell Laurie 'I read atoms' and rank human life beside rubble. It then asks what grounds morality's authority over a being no one can punish, rejecting divine command theory (Manhattan's 'clock without a craftsman') and doubting Kant's rational grounding applies to someone lacking moral concepts, so 'no one is above the moral law' may rest on a brute fact. It closes on political morality: a United States made a hyperpower by Manhattan's service (as in his Vietnam intervention) may not claim a double standard, since sovereignty blocks preventive war even when the US would win at little cost.

chapters.file: ch06 - H O N O R.md
chapters.relation: This file gathers three Part One essays. Jacob Held reads Rorschach's 'evil must be punished' credo (drowning Big Figure, executing the multiple rapist) as Kantian retributivism: wrongdoers are punished because they deserve it, out of respect for their dignity and honor, punishment restoring the moral order (with Hegel) — and Rorschach's flaw is lacking the humility and checks that keep just deserts from degenerating into the Black Freighter's vengeance. Tony Spanakos applies Max Weber's definition of the state as the monopoly of legitimate violence to argue the Keene Act rightly criminalizes vigilantes like Rorschach and Veidt, and that even state-sanctioned heroes (the Comedian gunning down his pregnant Vietnamese lover, Dr. Manhattan's amoral ending of Vietnam) show a badge cannot make superhero coercion legitimate. J. Keeping reconstructs Nietzsche's Übermensch — confronting the death of God and nihilism, creating values by 'giving style' to one's character via the camel-lion-child metamorphoses — and tests each Watchman against it, concluding only self-created Ozymandias comes close, though his mass murder is mere utilitarianism rather than genuine value creation.

chapters.file: ch07 - P A R T T W O.md
chapters.relation: Three Part Two essays. Robert Loftis argues Moore and Gibbons use Ozymandias's squid attack to indict consequentialism — Veidt uses New York's dead as mere means to world peace, and Dr. Manhattan's 'Nothing ever ends' shows the utilitarian ledger dissolves into an infinite future — while Rorschach's 'never compromise' mantra is a counterfeit deontology rationalizing fascist thuggery, the comic's real target being anyone who sets himself up as guardian of society ('Who watches the watchmen?'). Mark White argues the potbellied second Nite Owl is the truest hero on Aristotelian terms: his courage in the tenement fire and the prison break hits the mean between Laurie's caution and Rorschach's recklessness, making him a flourishing moral exemplar whom John Doris's situationism fails to unseat. Alex Nuttall asks whether Rorschach was wrong to walk out and expose Veidt, using Kant's murderer-at-the-door case to show there is a duty not to lie but no duty to tell the truth (blame falls on Veidt), while act and rule utilitarianism both counsel silence.

chapters.file: ch08 - P A R T T H R E E.md
chapters.relation: James DiGiovanna uses Dr. Manhattan's origin — disintegration in the intrinsic field chamber and self-reassembly — plus his teleportations to Mars and his split into three simultaneous selves, to run the classic personal identity debates. Descartes's immaterial thinking substance, Hume's mere bundle of perceptions, and Locke's memory theory are tested against a being who remembers in both time directions and rebuilds his body from pure thought ('restructuring myself after the subtraction of my intrinsic field was the first trick I learned'); Parfit's teletransporter, physical and psychological criteria, and fission cases — mirrored in Nagel's split-brain patients — then show ordinary people cannot say whether they would survive teleporting or bisection. The chapter concludes Dr. Manhattan is the only being with fully secure identity, since his consciousness needs neither body nor an unbroken spatiotemporal path and he can encompass several points of view at once.

chapters.file: ch09 - H E N R I B E R G S O N.md
chapters.relation: Three Part Three essays on Dr. Manhattan's strange relation to time and fate. Christopher Drohan reads Manhattan's simultaneous 'intricately structured jewel' of time through Bergson's Matter and Memory — perception interlaced with memory, the pure past persisting in every act, time as lived duration — so that 'Nothing ever ends, Adrian' becomes a Bergsonian insight and the thermodynamic-miracle speech an intuition of life's creative improbability. Arthur Ward argues theological fatalism (Boethius and Aquinas placing a timeless God outside time, Paley's watchmaker behind Jon the watchmaker's son with his clock-shaped Martian palace) does not doom Laurie's free will, because Jon's own claims are inconsistent — he is surprised by the cancer rumors, misses Veidt's tachyon-shielded plan, and acts drugged — so either his foresight or his fatalism must be false. Andrew Terjesen reads Manhattan as a Stoic sage: Seneca and Epictetus on emotions as false judgments explain his 'a live body and a dead body contain the same number of particles,' his Mars epiphany is the sage's 'good emotion' of joy at the thermodynamic miracle, and his impersonal 'clock without a craftsman' completes a Neo-Stoic line running through Descartes to Spinoza's God-who-is-Nature.

chapters.file: ch10 - P A R T F O U R.md
chapters.relation: Four Part Four essays beyond ethics. Aaron Meskin asks whether Watchmen is literature at all, testing definitions from Beardsley, Eagleton, Lamarque/Olsen and Hirsch in the Socratic 'what is X?' way, and concludes the question is indeterminate because comics are a hybrid art form — though the book's literary allusions (Shelley's 'Ozymandias,' Blake's 'Tyger,' Burroughs) deserve literary appreciation regardless. Sarah Donovan and Nick Richardson read the two Silk Spectres through three feminisms: Sally and Laurie as liberal feminists (Wollstonecraft, Mill) who fight crime, their hypersexual costumes as Irigaray-style subversive mimicry of gender stereotypes that risks reinforcing them (the Silhouette's expulsion exposing the heterosexual norm), the Comedian's attempted rape exposing 'she asked for it' attitudes, and Laurie as Beauvoir's woman in bad faith, living out her mother's fantasies until she finally names and dresses herself. Robert Arp uses Hooded Justice and Captain Metropolis's closeted relationship to dismantle 'homosexuality is unnatural' arguments — the ideal-function view would condemn the infertile too, and Hume's is-ought point undermines the procreation argument — before defending gay marriage against slippery-slope and parenting objections. Taneli Kukkonen maps Kierkegaard's stages onto the Comedian's mocking irony (hiding even his paternity of Laurie and his Kennedy confession as jokes) and Rorschach's deeper humor of the ethical stage, a knight of resignation whose 'never compromise, not even in the face of Armageddon' expects nothing back from the world.

holes.name: Monopoly on Legitimate Violence
holes.what: Max Weber's thesis that a state is a human community that successfully claims the monopoly of the legitimate use of physical force within a given territory.
holes.why: Chapter 6's Keene Act essay evaluates whether Rorschach's and Veidt's vigilantism, or state-employed heroes' coercion, can ever be legitimate, and that whole argument is framed by this Weberian criterion, which taxonomy lacks.

holes.name: Philosophy of Art (Aesthetics)
holes.what: The branch of philosophy that asks what art (and here literature) is and how classificatory categories like 'novel' or 'hybrid art form' apply to borderline works.
holes.why: Chapter 10's opening essay tests rival definitions of literature (Beardsley, Eagleton, Lamarque/Olsen, Hirsch) to decide whether Watchmen counts as a novel, and taxonomy has no aesthetics or definition-of-art slug beyond Kant's judgment of taste.
